prompt: Why didn't Harvard have calculus classes when it first opened?
answer:
Harvard did not offer calculus when it opened in 1638 because **calculus had not yet been developed as a recognized subject**. Newton and Leibniz created their versions of the calculus only in the 1660s and 1670s, decades after Harvard began instruction.

Harvard’s early curriculum was modeled on English universities and emphasized the classical liberal arts—Latin and Greek, rhetoric, logic, theology, ethics, and philosophy. Mathematics was present, but mainly as **arithmetic and geometry**, with some astronomy. In the original three-year course, mathematics was confined largely to the final year.

By the eighteenth century, as Newtonian science became influential, Harvard began teaching more advanced mathematics. Instruction in calculus—then often called **“fluxions”**—was established particularly under Professor John Winthrop, appointed in 1738. Thus, calculus was absent at Harvard’s founding both because it was not yet available as a developed field and because the College’s initial educational priorities were classical and theological rather than advanced scientific.
